slides.title:
Using ADKAR with
Context and Evidence
slides.notes: Good afternoon. We are Class 2 Group 4. Today we will use ADKAR to examine a management problem at a fictional retailer, Cedar Retail. We keep ADKAR’s five outcomes and propose a decision record that makes working conditions and responsibilities explicit. This is a formal training session for managers. We will explain the model, examine its limits, show our proposed record and practise making a decision. Our proposal has not been tested in a real organisation.

body: How will people question and practise it?

slides.notes: The session has six sections. We begin with the retail case and our objectives. We then explain ADKAR and four limitations of using its five outcomes as a standalone checklist. Next, we show our proposed decision record. Research provides a basis for the design and also sets limits on our claims. Finally, you will apply the approach in a short discussion and a team office activity. We will close with recommendations and questions.

slides.title: Cedar Retail: the change
body: A fictional retailer introduces barcode stock receiving across two shifts.
Receive a delivery, identify a stock mismatch and report it correctly.
The evening shift lacks reliable scanner access and protected practice time.
Inherited stock errors may reduce the colleague's performance rating.
slides.notes: Cedar Retail is a fictional retailer introducing digital stock receiving. A colleague must receive a delivery, scan stock and report a mismatch. On the evening shift, the scanner is unreliable and the roster provides no protected practice time. The colleague also questions penalties for inherited stock errors. This gives managers both an individual learning question and organisational issues to resolve. We use the case for teaching. It contains no real company data or observed business results.

slides.title: Three manager objectives
body: Identify an individual ADKAR barrier and the support it calls for.
Link the affected task to organisational conditions and accountable owners.
Explain continue, revise or pause using evidence and prerequisites.
slides.notes: By the end, a manager should be able to do three things. First, identify the person’s individual ADKAR need and choose relevant support. Second, connect that need to the task’s working conditions and accountable owners. Third, use task evidence to decide whether to continue, revise the design or pause an affected task. These objectives guide our record and the classroom activity. Completing the activity shows understanding of the scenario, rather than proof of ability in an actual workplace.

slides.title: The original ADKAR model
body: Willingness to participate and support it
Explain and teach the new task
slides.notes: ADKAR describes five outcomes of individual change. Awareness means understanding why change is needed. Desire concerns willingness to participate. Knowledge concerns how to change. Ability means applying the relevant skills and behaviours. Reinforcement supports continued use. A manager assesses the person’s needs and provides suitable support, starting with the earliest barrier. Training, coaching and repeated assessment already belong to the baseline approach. We do not present those existing provisions as inventions of our team.

slides.title: ADKAR and the wider method
body:
Shared language
Earliest barrier
Targeted individual support
Repeated assessment

PCT: success, sponsorship and project health
3-Phase Process: prepare, manage and sustain
ADKAR: individual adoption
slides.notes: We distinguish ADKAR from the wider Prosci Methodology. ADKAR helps managers identify individual support needs. The wider methodology also includes organisational process, sponsorship and project health through the PCT and the 3-Phase Process. Ability can involve external working conditions. Our criticism therefore concerns using the five outcomes alone as a checklist. We do not claim that the wider Prosci approach ignores organisations. Beryl will now explain the remaining gaps and how they inform our proposal.

slides.title: 01 / Shared working conditions
body: Ability can involve external conditions. Individual support remains relevant.
The five outcomes alone do not allocate coupled conditions across organisational owners.
Scanner access belongs to IT. Protected practice time belongs to the store manager.
slides.notes: Our first limitation concerns shared working conditions. ADKAR recognises that Ability can depend on external conditions. However, a five-outcome checklist does not itself allocate responsibility across IT, a store manager and a sponsor. At Cedar Retail, the IT lead owns scanner access and the manager owns practice time. Our added conditions record makes those responsibilities explicit for the affected task. Weiner and the multilevel readiness literature support considering collective conditions. They do not validate our particular record.

slides.title: 02 / A reasonable objection
body: The colleague supports better stock records but questions the penalty rule.
A Desire barrier does not itself require a sponsor to review the design.
Record the concern and alternative. Require a reasoned retain, revise or stop decision.
slides.notes: The second limitation concerns a reasonable objection to the design. A colleague may support better stock records and still question a penalty rule. Piderit’s work on ambivalence and research on resistance help explain why a mixed response deserves investigation. Our addition requires the sponsor to record a reasoned decision about the concern. The sponsor may retain, revise or stop the disputed rule. We must investigate whether the rule is unfair. The fictional colleague’s concern alone does not establish that conclusion.

slides.title: 03 / Dependencies across roles
body: The earliest personal barrier guides the colleague's support.
IT and the store manager can resolve enabling conditions in parallel.
A personal sequence alone does not schedule the linked work across roles.
slides.notes: The third limitation concerns dependencies across roles. Individual support and organisational work may need to happen together. A colleague can learn the procedure while IT repairs access and the manager arranges practice. A dependency register links each enabling condition to the task that depends on it, its owner and completion evidence. Systems and contextual change research inform this design. We keep the individual ADKAR assessment and add a route for work that crosses organisational roles.

slides.title: Four limitations, four additions
body: L2: justified challenge to the design
slides.notes: The fourth limitation concerns conflicting evidence. A colleague’s readiness rating, a task demonstration and actual working conditions may tell different stories. Our evidence rule requires the manager to investigate that conflict and keep readiness unverified until relevant evidence supports the task decision. This slide matches each gap to one addition: conditions and ownership, a reasoned sponsor response, dependency routing and the evidence rule. These are proposed management rules. They are not new validated measures of readiness.

slides.title: Our modified decision tool
body: Individual ADKAR needs and relevant support
A justified task decision, named owners and a review trigger
slides.notes: Our proposed tool keeps the individual ADKAR assessment. It adds conditions, employee concerns, dependencies and task evidence to one decision record. The manager then records a decision, its reason, a named owner and a review trigger. A review may lead to continuing, revising the design or pausing the affected task. We build on existing ideas rather than replacing the complete Prosci Methodology. The record’s usefulness and the time it requires still need to be tested.

slides.title: The dependency register
body: Successful login on the actual shift
slides.notes: The dependency register links an upstream condition to a dependent action. Scanner access supports practice, and a successful login on the actual shift provides completion evidence. Protected time supports realistic practice, with the roster and completed task as evidence. The sponsor’s response clarifies the disputed rule. We assign each action to an organisational role. These roles are different from our student presentation roles. A completed entry requires evidence, rather than a promise that the owner will act later.

slides.title: One complete decision record
body: Which change, role, shift and specific task?
Which ADKAR need and relevant action?
What is missing or disputed, and who owns it?
What must happen first, and what is verified?
Continue, revise or pause, with a reason and trigger
slides.notes: The complete record asks five sets of questions. What is the task and whose work is affected? Which individual ADKAR need requires support? What condition or concern needs an owner? What must happen first, and what evidence is available? Finally, what decision follows and when will the manager review it? Keep the record focused on one task so it remains usable. The record supports a reasoned discussion. It does not calculate a validated readiness score.

slides.title: Implementation and owners
body: Agree the task, scope and evidence criteria
Allocate conditions and answer the concern
Observe the task in usable conditions
Record the decision and follow-up trigger
slides.notes: Implementation starts by agreeing the task and evidence criteria with the colleague. The relevant owners then address conditions and respond to concerns. Some actions can run in parallel. The colleague practises in usable conditions, and the manager observes the representative task. Finally, the manager records a decision and review trigger. These steps prevent an assigned action from being mistaken for completed work. Our classroom example illustrates the process. It does not demonstrate a completed implementation.

slides.title: Continue, revise or pause
body: Hold the affected task and resolve it
The design is disputed or unsuitable
Prerequisites and task evidence are verified
slides.notes: Our proposed decision rules have three outcomes. Continue when the necessary conditions and task evidence support proceeding with follow-up. Revise when the design needs a reasoned change. Pause the affected task when an essential prerequisite is missing. A task-level pause does not stop the entire change project. Training and repairs may continue while the task remains on hold. The decision record must explain the scope and what evidence would allow the manager to reconsider it.

slides.notes: The proposal uses one shared digital record and existing manager, IT and sponsor roles. This may make responsibilities easier to follow, but it also takes time to maintain. A pilot should examine task accuracy, unresolved dependencies, the quality of responses to concerns and the time spent updating the record. These are proposed evaluation questions, not measured benefits. We should compare the approach with current practice before making claims about better outcomes.

slides.title: Research behind the decision record
body: Check performance in usable working conditions.
Training attendance alone does not verify Ability.
Invite questions and discuss mistakes without blame.
A safe discussion does not prove task competence.
Record a concern and assign a response owner.

slides.cites: Baldwin and Ford 1988; Edmondson 1999; Morrison 2023
slides.notes: Three research areas inform our design. Baldwin and Ford distinguish learning from its transfer to work. Edmondson links psychological safety with team learning behaviour. Morrison reviews employee voice and silence. These ideas support observing realistic work, discussing mistakes and recording responses to concerns. None of these studies tests our Cedar Retail record. They support our design choices, while the effectiveness of the combined tool remains unverified.

slides.title: Conclusion
body: Use ADKAR to identify relevant support.
Name the conditions, owners and dependencies.
Answer concerns and verify task evidence.
slides.cites: Team synthesis informed by the cited literature; proposed adaptation remains untested
slides.notes: Our conclusion returns to the three objectives. ADKAR provides a useful language for individual support. Our proposed record makes organisational conditions, owners and dependencies explicit. It also requires a reasoned response to concerns and an evidence-based task decision. Managers can then explain why they continue, revise or pause an affected task. The proposal complements existing provision. We have shown its logic through a fictional case, rather than established its effectiveness in practice.

slides.title: Recommendations and design lesson
body: Agree the task, evidence criteria and accountable owners.
Compare decisions, unresolved conditions and maintenance time.
A useful diagnosis still needs clear delivery responsibilities.
slides.cites: Nilsen 2015; Stouten, Rousseau, and De Cremer 2018; team design synthesis
slides.notes: We recommend trying the record on one task before wider use. Agree the evidence criteria and accountable owners, then compare the decisions and maintenance burden with current practice. Our design lesson is that identifying an individual need does not complete the organisational work required to respond. This lesson comes from our analysis and comparison, not a claimed field trial or an invented personal experience. Thank you. The next two slides provide our references, and we welcome questions.
